Average session length by week
Top 100 products by sales last quarter

explanation: OLTP touches a few rows fast. The others scan large amounts of data.

prompt: Why is a column store fast for `SUM(amount)` over a year?

options.text: It keeps the whole table cached in RAM, so it never touches disk
It reads only the needed columns, which compress well, not whole rows
It walks a B-tree index on amount instead of scanning the table
It pre-computes every SUM at write time, so queries just look it up

explanation: A column store reads only the columns a query names, and same-typed columns compress very well, so bytes scanned drop sharply. It doesn't rely on RAM-caching everything, B-tree lookups (useless for full-year aggregates) or precomputing every possible SUM.

prompt: 1 billion rows, 50 columns of 8 bytes. About how much does a column store read for a query on 2 columns, before compression?

options.text: 400 GB
16 GB
8 GB
800 MB

explanation: 1e9 × 2 × 8 bytes = 16 GB, versus about 400 GB for a row store.

prompt: Why is this a poor fit?
scenario: A team moves the live shopping-cart table into a column-oriented warehouse so dashboards can query it directly. Adding an item to a cart now takes over a second, and update throughput collapses.

options.text: Column stores can't hold the JSON cart payloads, so each write is converted
Column stores are slow at frequent single-row updates; keep carts in OLTP
The warehouse needs more columns per cart so updates stay narrower
Column stores lack primary keys, so each update scans for the cart row

explanation: Column layouts trade single-row write speed for scan speed: an update touches every column file and writes are batched. Carts are a classic OLTP workload. Warehouses can store JSON and have keys, and adding columns makes writes worse, not better.

prompt: Which help column stores compress and scan fast? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dictionary encoding
Run-length encoding of sorted columns
Vectorised execution
Storing each row's values together

explanation: Storing rows together (d) is the row-store layout.

scenario: A finance dashboard runs a 6-minute GROUP BY over 300 million orders on the production Postgres primary every 15 minutes. Checkout p99 latency triples while it runs.

options.text: Give the primary more CPU and RAM so the report and checkout both fit
Move reporting off the primary: CDC or replica extracts to a warehouse
Schedule the report at midnight on the primary when traffic is quiet
Add an index on every column the GROUP BY touches to speed the scan

explanation: Long analytical scans compete with transactions for CPU, I/O and cache; a separate analytics path (CDC or extracts into a column store) removes the contention. More hardware only delays it, global users mean there is no quiet midnight, and indexes don't help a full aggregate and slow every write.

options.text: Nightly CSV exports of each table, loaded into the warehouse in bulk
Streaming inserts, updates and deletes from the DB log to other systems
A backup tool that snapshots the database files for point-in-time restore
An index type that records which rows changed since the last query

explanation: CDC reads the database's replication log and streams each change to other systems within seconds or minutes. Nightly CSV dumps are batch extracts, snapshots are backups, and it isn't an index.

prompt: What do lakehouse table formats like Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake add to files in object storage?

options.text: Faster SSD-backed disks under the bucket so file reads have lower latency
Table metadata with transactions, schema evolution and time travel
A row-oriented layout so single-row updates become cheap on the lake
A built-in BI dashboard layer that queries the files with no engine

explanation: Iceberg and Delta add a metadata layer that makes a set of files behave like a reliable table: atomic commits, schema evolution and time travel. They don't change the storage hardware, files stay columnar (Parquet), and you still need a query engine.

scenario: A fleet of 3,000 servers sends 400 metrics each every 10 seconds. Dashboards show the last hour at full resolution and the last year as hourly averages.

options.text: A row-store table with one row per reading, indexed on time, kept forever
A time-series DB with time partitions, compression, downsampling, retention
A graph database linking each server node to its metric readings
Raw files in object storage only, scanned directly by the dashboards

explanation: Time-series stores are built for high append rates, time-range queries, compression and ageing data out via downsampling and retention. A forever row table grows without bound, a graph model fits relationships not series, and raw files with no engine can't serve dashboards.
